candidates.name: Palazzo Reale
candidates.content: The Palace was built in the 16th century, modernised in the 17th and converted to a museum in 1946. The result is a wacky hybrid of medieval, baroque and bling. You enter via the palace gardens to reach the ticket office. The tick

candidates.name: Museo Egizio
candidates.content: "The road to Memphis and Thebes passes through Turin" said Egyptologist Jean-François Champollion about Museo Egizio in Turin, second only in order of importance to the one in Cairo. Many artifacts were collected by Bernardino Dro

candidates.name: Mole Antonelliana
candidates.content: The Mole, Turin's landmark building built in 1888, was intended as a synagogue but the size and cost got out of hand and the Jewish community never used it. The 167.5-metre tower is the highest work of masonry in Europe and you ca

candidates.name: Museum of Oriental Art
candidates.content: This museum houses art from Kandahar, India, Southeast Asia, China and Japan. The third floor shows Buddhist and Tibetan culture. The fourth floor is Islamic and Arabian, mainly bronzes, ceramics and tiles.

candidates.name: Museum of the Shroud
candidates.content: The original Sindone or Turin Shroud is in safekeeping in the Cathedral and rarely displayed. This small museum displays a copy and studies the Shroud. It's a remarkable object whatever it is, a 4.4 x 1.1 m winding sheet charred b

candidates.name: Palazzo Barolo
candidates.content: Baroque bling palace, visit by guided tour. Its last private owner Carlo Tancredi Falletti di Barolo served Napoleon then worked tirelessly for relief of the poor; his palace then became an opera house.

candidates.name: Pietro Micca Museum
candidates.content: In 1706 the French besieged Turin for four months as part of the War of Spanish Succession, which embroiled all major European powers and their colonies. The defending Savoyards had dug 15 km of counter-sapping tunnels, to prevent

candidates.name: Pinacoteca Giovanni e Marella Agnelli
candidates.content: Striking modern building, maybe an orbiter's solar power module? - perched atop the Lingotti Centre. It houses the Agnelli's private art collection, with many big names represented.

candidates.name: Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist
candidates.alt: Duomo; Cattedrale di San Giovanni Battista
candidates.content: Large elegant cathedral dating from late 15th century, enlarged in the 17th to create the Chapel for the Shroud of Turin. However this chapel (rebuilt after a fire in 1997) is nowadays accessed as part of a tour of Palazzo Reale a

candidates.name: Santa Maria di Monte dei Cappuccini
candidates.content: A late-Renaissance-style church on a hill overlooking the River Po. It was built 1583 to 1656 for the Capuchin Friars; the delay was through plague and the occasional war. A miracle supposedly occurred in 1640 during the French as

candidates.name: Basilica di Maria Ausiliatrice
candidates.alt: Basilica of Our Lady Help of Christians
candidates.content: Palladian church built 1865-68, originally as part of a care facility for poor and delinquent boys founded by Don Bosco (1815-88). He himself is buried here, along with 6000 bits and pieces of saints.

candidates.name: Mausoleo della Bela Rosin
candidates.content: Rosa Vercellana (1833-1885) became the mistress of the future Victor Emmanuel II and had two children by him before she was 16. She was made a countess when his legitimate wife and queen died in 1855, and in 1869 when the king tho

candidates.name: Villa della Regina
candidates.content: A royal palace and gardens on a hill east edge of the city. It's modest by Savoyard standards but plush with Chinese and Baroque interiors. This reflects the era of Anne Marie d'Orléans, in residence from 1692. Next to the Villa,

candidates.name: Moncalieri Castle
candidates.content: This castle was built as a fortress by Thomas I of Savoy, but enlarged into a pleasure palace in the mid-15th century. From the 19th century it was especially used by queen mothers and princesses. Today it houses the Carabinieri,

candidates.name: Foundation Accorsi-Ometto
candidates.content: Extensive display of furniture, painting and other decorative art.

candidates.name: Galleria Civica d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea
candidates.content: Huge permanent collection of 19th and 20th century art.

candidates.name: Museo Nazionale dell'Automobile
candidates.content: The collection houses over 170 vehicles, from 18th-century carriages to Formula 1 racers, and lots of gorgeous red sports cars.

candidates.name: Museum of Criminal Anthropology
candidates.content: Cesare Lombroso (1835-1909) was convinced that criminality was inherited, little influenced by environment and that criminals could be distinguished by their ugly atavistic features. It therefore followed that any ethnic group tha

candidates.name: Museum of The New Prison
candidates.content: Spooky museum of prisons and punishments. Visit by guided tour; booking is recommended, and essential for the descent into the air raid shelter.

candidates.name: Chapel of the Merchants
candidates.alt: Cappella dei Mercanti, Negozianti e Banchieri
candidates.content: A jewel of baroque architecture and sacred art built from 1680 by businessmen anxious to sanctify their dealings - they were, let's stress, "The Pious Congregation of Bankers, Shopkeepers and Merchants of Turin." One theme of the

candidates.name: Chiesa Maria Santissima Del Carmelo
candidates.content: This church was built in the 1730s for a Carmelite convent.

candidates.name: Museo Nazionale della Montagna Duca degli Abruzzi
candidates.content: History of alpine mountaineering.

candidates.name: Museo Ettore Fico
candidates.content: Only open for temporary exhibitions, but with a small permanent display of the work of Ettore Fico (1917-2004).

candidates.name: Palazzina di Caccia di Stupinigi
candidates.content: Royal hunting lodge built from 1729, and like Veneria Reale its embellishments then got out of hand to create something a Disney princess would swoon over, grand halls and galleries and salons with putti and nymphs in industrial q

candidates.name: Museo Civico d'Arte Antica
candidates.content: This museum is within Palazzo Madama on Piazza Castello. It's misnamed, as the art collection is Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque, and more ancient (eg Byzantine) work is elsewhere.

candidates.name: Risorgimento Museum
candidates.content: Fascinating exposition of the tumultuous birth of modern Italy, set in the very building where many events took place: Carlo Alberto and Vittorio Emanuele II were born here, and the first Italian parliament sat here. Garibaldi's c

candidates.name: Galleria d'Italia
candidates.content: Galleria d'Italia is a museum chain to show off the art owned by Intesa Sanpaolo bank, the modern nobility. The Turin branch, opened in 2022, is in the Palazzo Turinetti di Pertengo and mostly displays photography. Their others ar

candidates.name: La Venaria Reale
candidates.content: Built as a royal hunting lodge from 1675, this grew and grew into a humonguous bling palace, trying to outshine Versailles. It became a barracks and was knocked about in Napoleonic times, remaining military until the 1930s, then t

candidates.name: Teatro Regio
candidates.content: The city opera house is active Oct-June. It was opened in 1740 but burned down in 1936. Reconstruction took until 1973, with a modern building behind the original facade, seating 1500.

candidates.name: Teatro Carignano
candidates.content: The city's oldest and premier theatre, opened in 1753. It was wrecked by fire in 1786 but swiftly rebuilt to the original plan, and from 1936 to 1973 it was the opera house during Teatro Regio's lengthy closure.

candidates.name: Juventus FC
candidates.content: "Juve", founded in 1897, play soccer in Serie A, Italy's top tier, and have almost never been out of the top flight. Allianz Stadium, capacity 41,000, has a club museum.

candidates.name: Torino FC
candidates.content: "Toro" also play in Serie A. The original club was founded in 1906 and dominated until 1949, when team and staff died in the Superga air crash. They had mixed fortunes thereafter and went bust in 2005, so this is a phoenix club. T

candidates.name: Teatro Colosseo
candidates.content: A modern concert hall seating 1500.

candidates.name: Birrificio Torino
candidates.content: Brewpub restaurant with six beers brewed on premises. Good menu with recommended matched beers. More restaurant than pub, it can be very busy.

candidates.name: Caffe Rossini
candidates.content: Calls itself a restaurant, but it's really a café and late-night pub with music and a young crowd.

candidates.name: Lab Vittorio
candidates.content: Small lively bar with good cocktails and tapas. They have another bar at Via Mazzini 5.

candidates.name: Caffe al Bicerin
candidates.content: Home of the classic Torinese drink, the Bicerin, a mix of coffee, hot chocolate and cream. But pricey and long queues.

candidates.name: Grom
candidates.content: Renowned ice cream chain. Their other outlets are on Via Accademia delle Scienze, Via Garibaldi, Corso Romania and Via Nizza.

candidates.name: Piola Cianci
candidates.content: Popular place for fast inexpensive antipasti and main meals.

candidates.name: Focacceria Lagrange
candidates.content: Nice place to eat light and crispy focaccia. Fast service. Mostly takeaway but they have a few tables inside and out.

candidates.name: Gofreria Piemontèisa
candidates.content: Gofri are waffles Piedmont style, thin with sweet or savoury fillings.

candidates.name: La Stuzzicheria
candidates.content: Good local good pizza and excellent farinata.

candidates.name: Bicyclette
candidates.content: Impressive variety of sweet and savory crepes; high quality dough and ingredients.

candidates.name: Pizzeria Ristorante Gonzales Torino
candidates.content: Simple local pizzeria, can feel crowded and grubby.

candidates.name: Trattoria San Domenico
candidates.content: Traditional Italian food, with Sardinian specialities.

candidates.name: Antica Bruschetteria Pautasso
candidates.content: Specialises in local Piedmont dishes, including bagna cauda.

candidates.name: Gelateria Pepino
candidates.content: An ice-cream parlor founded in 1884. They were personal favorites of Benito Mussolini, and during his regime Pepino sent daily ice-cream deliveries to the dictator in Rome.

candidates.name: Mezzaluna
candidates.price: Antipasti for €7, primi and secondi for €12
candidates.content: Friendly staff serving vegan versions of Italian and other dishes.

candidates.name: Ristorante Del Cambio
candidates.content: A posh restaurant serving Piemontese delicacies, occasional flops but mostly great reviews. They even offer a tasting menu for vegetarians. You want to be in the palatial main dining salon not in Farmacia cafe or Cavour bar.

candidates.name: Porta Palazzo
candidates.content: Big street and indoor market for food produce, clothes, houseware, ethnic products, handicrafts and second-hand articles. On the second Sunday of each month there's a smaller antiques and flea market called Gran Balôn.

december.text: Cioccola in the first week of December is all about chocolate, and why you ought to buy more of it for Christmas.
